# Choosing and Configuring Origins for a CloudFront Distribution

## Overview

When you create a distribution, you specify the origin where CloudFront sends requests for the files. CloudFront can use an Amazon S3 bucket, a MediaStore container, a MediaPackage channel, an Application Load Balancer, or an AWS Lambda function URL as an origin. API Gateway can also be used as a custom origin. When you create a CloudFront distribution, CloudFront automatically configures most distribution settings based on your content origin type.

You can use CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge to route requests to different origins based on factors such as the viewer's geographic location, request headers, or query string parameters.

For high availability, origin failover designates a primary origin plus a second origin that CloudFront automatically switches to when the primary origin returns specific HTTP status code failure responses. To configure it, you specify an origin group for your CloudFront origin.

## VPC origins

An Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer, or EC2 instance in a private subnet can be used as a VPC origin. With VPC origins, applications can be accessed only in a private subnet with a CloudFront distribution, which prevents the application from being accessible on the public internet.

## Amazon S3 origins

Using an existing Amazon S3 bucket as a CloudFront origin doesn't change the bucket in any way. You incur regular Amazon S3 charges for storing objects in the bucket. For an S3 bucket to work with CloudFront, the bucket name must conform to DNS naming requirements.

When specifying an S3 bucket as an origin, the recommended format is bucket-name.s3.region.amazonaws.com. When the bucket is specified in this format, you can:

- configure CloudFront to communicate with the bucket using SSL/TLS;
- use origin access control to require viewers to access content using CloudFront URLs rather than Amazon S3 URLs; and
- update bucket content by submitting POST and PUT requests to CloudFront.

You should not specify the bucket using the path-style format s3.amazonaws.com/bucket-name or the Amazon S3 CNAME.

CloudFront supports S3 origins using any storage class, including S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Using CloudFront with S3 Intelligent-Tiering doesn't impact the performance or functionality of the distribution.

### Cost, speed, and CORS

Using CloudFront can be more cost effective than serving directly from S3 if users access objects frequently, because at higher usage the CloudFront data transfer price is lower than the S3 data transfer price. Downloads are also faster with CloudFront than with Amazon S3 alone because objects are stored closer to users. For CloudFront to respect Amazon S3 cross-origin resource sharing settings, CloudFront must be configured to forward the Origin header to Amazon S3.

### Object Lambda Access Points

Amazon S3 automatically generates a unique alias for an Object Lambda Access Point when it is created, and this alias can be used instead of a bucket name as a CloudFront origin. When you use an Object Lambda Access Point as an origin, you must use origin access control. CloudFront treats an Object Lambda Access Point origin the same as a standard Amazon S3 bucket origin. If you use Amazon S3 Object Lambda as an origin, you must configure four permissions: on the Object Lambda Access Point, the S3 Access Point, the S3 bucket, and the Lambda function.

### S3 Access Points

Amazon S3 also automatically generates a unique alias for an S3 Access Point, which can be used instead of a bucket name as a CloudFront origin. When you use an Amazon S3 Access Point as an origin, you must use origin access control. CloudFront treats an S3 Access Point origin the same as a standard Amazon S3 bucket origin.

### S3 Multi-Region Access Points

An Amazon S3 Multi-Region Access Point can be used as a CloudFront origin. These access points provide a global endpoint that automatically routes requests to the closest S3 bucket based on network latency. When using one as an origin, you specify its hostname, multi-region-access-point-alias.accesspoint.s3-global.amazonaws.com, as the origin domain name.

### S3 website endpoints

An S3 bucket configured as a website endpoint can be used as a custom origin with CloudFront. When using the S3 website endpoint format as the origin, you can use Amazon S3 redirects and custom error documents. If you use the CloudFront API to create a distribution with an S3 bucket configured as a website endpoint, you must configure it by using CustomOriginConfig.

### Adding CloudFront to an S3 bucket that uses your own domain name

If you distribute content from S3 using your own domain name, you can add CloudFront with no disruption by following the documented procedure. To keep using your own domain name to reference objects instead of the CloudFront domain name, you need to update your settings with your DNS service provider.

For Amazon S3 CNAMEs to work, the DNS service provider must have a CNAME resource record set that currently routes queries for the domain to the S3 bucket. To route queries to CloudFront instead of S3, you must update the CNAME resource record set for your domain to point to the CloudFront domain name. If you use Route 53 as your DNS service, you can use either a CNAME resource record set or an alias resource record set.

After you update the CNAME resource record set, it can take up to 72 hours for the change to propagate throughout the DNS system, although it usually happens faster. During propagation, some requests continue to be routed to the S3 bucket and others are routed to CloudFront.

### Moving a bucket to a different Region

CloudFront can take up to an hour to update its records for a moved bucket's new Region when both conditions hold: you use an origin access identity (OAI) to restrict bucket access, and you move the bucket to an S3 Region that requires Signature Version 4. This is because, when using OAIs, CloudFront uses the Region, among other values, to calculate the signature it uses to request objects from the bucket. Updating the CloudFront distribution, for example its Description field, forces a faster update because CloudFront immediately checks the Region of the bucket. Propagation of a distribution update to all edge locations should take only a few minutes.

## Application Load Balancer origins

CloudFront can route traffic to both internal and internet-facing Application Load Balancers. An internet-facing load balancer has a publicly resolvable DNS name and routes requests from clients to targets over the internet. VPC origins can deliver content from applications hosted with an internal Application Load Balancer in VPC private subnets and prevent the application from being accessible on the public internet.

## Network Load Balancer origins

You can use both internal and internet-facing Network Load Balancers with CloudFront. Internal Network Load Balancers inside private subnets can be used with CloudFront by using VPC origins.

## Lambda function URL origins

A Lambda function URL is a dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a Lambda function. A Lambda web application can be invoked directly through the function URL with no need to integrate with API Gateway or an Application Load Balancer. To use a function URL as the origin, you specify the full domain name of the function URL as the origin domain. The function URL must be publicly accessible.

If you use OAC with a Lambda function URL, the AuthType parameter must be AWS_IAM and a resource-based policy must allow lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions. If you don't use OAC, you can set the function URL AuthType to NONE and allow the lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl permission in a resource-based policy. Adding a custom origin header and writing function code to return an error if the header is absent helps ensure users can only access the web application through CloudFront and not directly via the Lambda function URL.

## Lambda Web Function origins

A Lambda Web Function is a web application that runs on AWS Lambda and provides its own HTTPS endpoint, which can be regional or global. You can use one as the origin for a CloudFront distribution by specifying the hostname of its endpoint as the origin domain. A regional endpoint (HomeRegion and PerRegion types) has a hostname ending in .lambda-web.AWS-Region.on.aws, while a global endpoint (MultiRegion type) has a hostname ending in .lambda-web.global.on.aws.

To use OAC with a Lambda Web Function, the endpoint's auth type must be IamAuth, and the function's resource-based policy must allow the lambda:InvokeWebFunctionEndpoint permission. CloudFront signs requests to regional endpoints with SigV4 and to global endpoints with SigV4a.

## EC2 and custom origins

You can use both internal and internet-facing EC2 instances with CloudFront, and internal instances in private subnets work via VPC origins. It is recommended to use an Elastic Load Balancing load balancer to handle traffic across multiple EC2 instances and isolate the application from EC2 instance changes. When using a load balancer in front of EC2 instances, you specify the load balancer URL as the domain name of the origin server.

A custom origin is an HTTP(S) web server with a publicly resolvable DNS name that routes requests from clients to targets over the internet. An Amazon S3 origin configured as a website endpoint is considered a custom origin. Most CloudFront features are supported with a custom origin except private content. For CloudFront to access a custom origin, the origin must remain publicly accessible, even though signed URLs can be used to distribute content from it.

## Time zone

CloudFront uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) for signed URLs, signed cookies, logs, and reports, and CloudWatch also uses UTC.

# Using CloudFront origins

## Before you begin

If you plan to use an S3 Object Lambda Access Point as your origin, set up the following first:

- An S3 Object Lambda Access Point, with its generated alias, to use as the origin. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/olap-create.html
- An Amazon S3 Access Point that supports the Object Lambda Access Point.
- The Amazon S3 bucket behind the access point. You will edit its bucket policy.
- The AWS Lambda function used by the Object Lambda Access Point.
- A CloudFront origin access control (OAC), which is required for Object Lambda and S3 Access Point origins. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html

## Origins overview

When you create a distribution, you specify the origin where CloudFront sends requests for the files. CloudFront can use an Amazon S3 bucket, a MediaStore container, a MediaPackage channel, an Application Load Balancer, or an AWS Lambda function URL as an origin. API Gateway can also be used as a custom origin. When you create a distribution, CloudFront automatically configures most distribution settings based on your content origin type.

You can use CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge to route requests to different origins based on factors such as the viewer's geographic location, request headers, or query string parameters.

For high availability, you can specify an origin group for your CloudFront origin to configure origin failover. Specifying an origin group is enough to give you origin failover, which designates a primary origin plus a second origin that CloudFront automatically switches to when the primary origin returns specific HTTP status code failure responses.

CloudFront uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) for signed URLs, signed cookies, logs, and reports, and CloudWatch also uses UTC.

## VPC origins

An Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer, or EC2 instance in a private subnet can be used as a VPC origin. With VPC origins, applications can be accessed only in a private subnet with a CloudFront distribution, which prevents the application from being accessible on the public internet. VPC origins can deliver content from applications hosted with an internal Application Load Balancer in VPC private subnets. Internal Network Load Balancers inside private subnets can be used with CloudFront by using VPC origins, and that is enough to keep the application off the public internet. Because a VPC origin keeps the application inaccessible on the public internet, it cannot be combined with the requirement that a custom origin remain publicly accessible (see "Custom origins" below).

## Amazon S3 origins

Using an existing Amazon S3 bucket as a CloudFront origin doesn't change the bucket in any way. You incur regular Amazon S3 charges for storing objects in the bucket. For an S3 bucket to work with CloudFront, the bucket name must conform to DNS naming requirements.

When specifying an S3 bucket as an origin, the recommended format is bucket-name.s3.region.amazonaws.com. When the bucket is specified in this format, you can configure CloudFront to communicate with the bucket using SSL/TLS, you can use origin access control to require viewers to access content using CloudFront URLs rather than Amazon S3 URLs, and you can update bucket content by submitting POST and PUT requests to CloudFront. You should not specify the bucket using the path-style format s3.amazonaws.com/bucket-name or the Amazon S3 CNAME.

CloudFront supports S3 origins using any storage class, including S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Using CloudFront with S3 Intelligent-Tiering doesn't impact the performance or functionality of the distribution.

Using CloudFront can be more cost effective than serving directly from S3 if users access objects frequently, because at higher usage the CloudFront data transfer price is lower than the S3 data transfer price. Downloads are also faster with CloudFront than with Amazon S3 alone because objects are stored closer to users.

For CloudFront to respect Amazon S3 cross-origin resource sharing settings, CloudFront must be configured to forward the Origin header to Amazon S3.

### S3 Object Lambda Access Point origins

Amazon S3 automatically generates a unique alias for an Object Lambda Access Point when it is created, and you can use that alias instead of a bucket name as a CloudFront origin. When you use an Object Lambda Access Point as an origin, you must use origin access control. With that in place, CloudFront treats the Object Lambda Access Point origin the same as a standard Amazon S3 bucket origin.

If you use Amazon S3 Object Lambda as an origin, you must configure four permissions: on the Object Lambda Access Point, the S3 Access Point, the S3 bucket, and the Lambda function.

### S3 Access Point origins

Amazon S3 automatically generates a unique alias for an S3 Access Point, which can be used instead of a bucket name as a CloudFront origin. When you use an Amazon S3 Access Point as an origin, you must use origin access control. With that in place, CloudFront treats an S3 Access Point origin the same as a standard Amazon S3 bucket origin.

### S3 Multi-Region Access Point origins

An Amazon S3 Multi-Region Access Point can be used as a CloudFront origin. S3 Multi-Region Access Points provide a global endpoint that automatically routes requests to the closest S3 bucket based on network latency. When using one as an origin, you specify its hostname, multi-region-access-point-alias.accesspoint.s3-global.amazonaws.com, as the origin domain name.

### S3 website endpoint origins

An S3 bucket configured as a website endpoint can be used as a custom origin with CloudFront. When using the S3 website endpoint format as the origin, you can use Amazon S3 redirects and custom error documents. If you use the CloudFront API to create a distribution with an S3 bucket configured as a website endpoint, you must configure it by using CustomOriginConfig.

### Moving a bucket to another Region

When using OAIs, CloudFront uses the Region, among other values, to calculate the signature it uses to request objects from the bucket. Because of this, CloudFront can take up to an hour to update its records for a moved bucket's new Region only when both conditions hold: you use an origin access identity (OAI) to restrict bucket access, and you move the bucket to an S3 Region that requires Signature Version 4. Updating the CloudFront distribution, for example its Description field, forces a faster update because CloudFront immediately checks the Region of the bucket. Propagation of a distribution update to all edge locations should take only a few minutes.

### Adding CloudFront to content served from S3 with your own domain name

If you distribute content from S3 using your own domain name, you can add CloudFront with no disruption by following the documented procedure. To keep using your own domain name to reference objects instead of the CloudFront domain name, you need to update your settings with your DNS service provider.

For Amazon S3 CNAMEs to work, the DNS service provider must have a CNAME resource record set that currently routes queries for the domain to the S3 bucket. To route queries to CloudFront instead of S3, you must update that CNAME resource record set to point to the CloudFront domain name. If you use Route 53 as your DNS service, you can use either a CNAME resource record set or an alias resource record set. After you update the record set, it can take up to 72 hours for the change to propagate throughout the DNS system, although it usually happens faster. During propagation, some requests continue to be routed to the S3 bucket and others are routed to CloudFront.

## Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer, and EC2 origins

CloudFront can route traffic to both internal and internet-facing Application Load Balancers. An internet-facing load balancer has a publicly resolvable DNS name and routes requests from clients to targets over the internet. You can use both internal and internet-facing Network Load Balancers with CloudFront. You can also use both internal and internet-facing EC2 instances, and internal instances in private subnets work via VPC origins.

It is recommended to use an Elastic Load Balancing load balancer to handle traffic across multiple EC2 instances and isolate the application from EC2 instance changes. When using a load balancer in front of EC2 instances, you specify the load balancer URL as the domain name of the origin server.

## Lambda function URL origins

A Lambda function URL is a dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a Lambda function. A Lambda web application can be invoked directly through the function URL with no need to integrate with API Gateway or an Application Load Balancer. To use a function URL as the origin, you specify its full domain name as the origin domain. The function URL must be publicly accessible.

If you use OAC with a Lambda function URL, the AuthType parameter must be AWS_IAM and a resource-based policy must allow lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions. If you don't use OAC, you can set the function URL AuthType to NONE and allow the lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl permission in a resource-based policy.

Adding a custom origin header and writing function code to return an error if the header is absent helps ensure users can only access the web application through CloudFront and not directly via the Lambda function URL. This holds only when the function URL is publicly accessible and OAC is used with AuthType set to AWS_IAM and the resource-based policy allowing the permissions above.

## Lambda Web Function origins

A Lambda Web Function is a web application that runs on AWS Lambda and provides its own HTTPS endpoint, which can be regional or global. You can use one as the origin for a CloudFront distribution by specifying the hostname of its endpoint as the origin domain. A regional endpoint (HomeRegion and PerRegion types) has a hostname ending in .lambda-web.AWS-Region.on.aws. A global endpoint (MultiRegion type) has a hostname ending in .lambda-web.global.on.aws.

To use OAC with a Lambda Web Function, the endpoint's auth type must be IamAuth, and the function's resource-based policy must allow the lambda:InvokeWebFunctionEndpoint permission. Setting the auth type to IamAuth is enough to bring that permission requirement into play. CloudFront signs requests to regional endpoints with SigV4 and to global endpoints with SigV4a.

## Custom origins

A custom origin is an HTTP(S) web server with a publicly resolvable DNS name that routes requests from clients to targets over the internet. An Amazon S3 origin configured as a website endpoint is considered a custom origin. For CloudFront to access a custom origin, the origin must remain publicly accessible, even though signed URLs can be used to distribute content from it. That public accessibility is enough to explain why most CloudFront features are supported with a custom origin except private content.

# Amazon CloudFront Origins

## Overview

When you create a distribution, you specify the origin where CloudFront sends requests for the files. CloudFront can use an Amazon S3 bucket, a MediaStore container, a MediaPackage channel, an Application Load Balancer, or an AWS Lambda function URL as an origin. API Gateway can also be used as a custom origin. When you create a CloudFront distribution, CloudFront automatically configures most distribution settings based on your content origin type.

An Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer, or EC2 instance in a private subnet can be used as a VPC origin. With VPC origins, applications can be accessed only in a private subnet with a CloudFront distribution, which prevents the application from being accessible on the public internet. You can also use CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge to route requests to different origins based on factors such as the viewer's geographic location, request headers, or query string parameters.

## Amazon S3 buckets as origins

Using an existing Amazon S3 bucket as a CloudFront origin doesn't change the bucket in any way, and you incur regular Amazon S3 charges for storing objects in the bucket. For an S3 bucket to work with CloudFront, the bucket name must conform to DNS naming requirements.

When specifying an S3 bucket as an origin, the recommended format is bucket-name.s3.region.amazonaws.com. When the bucket is specified in this format, you can configure CloudFront to communicate with the bucket using SSL/TLS, use origin access control to require viewers to access content using CloudFront URLs rather than Amazon S3 URLs, and update bucket content by submitting POST and PUT requests to CloudFront. You should not specify the bucket using the path-style format s3.amazonaws.com/bucket-name or the Amazon S3 CNAME.

CloudFront supports S3 origins using any storage class, including S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Using CloudFront with S3 Intelligent-Tiering doesn't impact the performance or functionality of the distribution.

### Object Lambda Access Points

Amazon S3 automatically generates a unique alias for an Object Lambda Access Point when it is created, and this alias can be used instead of a bucket name as a CloudFront origin. When you use an Object Lambda Access Point as an origin for CloudFront, you must use origin access control. CloudFront treats an Object Lambda Access Point origin the same as a standard Amazon S3 bucket origin. If you use Amazon S3 Object Lambda as an origin, you must configure four permissions: on the Object Lambda Access Point, the S3 Access Point, the S3 bucket, and the Lambda function.

### S3 Access Points

Amazon S3 automatically generates a unique alias for an S3 Access Point, which can be used instead of a bucket name as a CloudFront origin. When you use an Amazon S3 Access Point as an origin for CloudFront, you must use origin access control. CloudFront treats an Amazon S3 Access Point origin the same as a standard Amazon S3 bucket origin.

### S3 Multi-Region Access Points

An Amazon S3 Multi-Region Access Point can be used as a CloudFront origin. S3 Multi-Region Access Points provide a global endpoint that automatically routes requests to the closest S3 bucket based on network latency. When using one as an origin, you specify its hostname, multi-region-access-point-alias.accesspoint.s3-global.amazonaws.com, as the origin domain name.

### S3 website endpoints

An S3 bucket configured as a website endpoint can be used as a custom origin with CloudFront, and it is considered a custom origin. When using the S3 website endpoint format as the origin, you can use Amazon S3 redirects and custom error documents. If you use the CloudFront API to create a distribution with an S3 bucket configured as a website endpoint, you must configure it by using CustomOriginConfig.

### Cost and performance

Using CloudFront can be more cost effective than serving directly from S3 if users access objects frequently, because at higher usage the CloudFront data transfer price is lower than the S3 data transfer price. Downloads are also faster with CloudFront than with Amazon S3 alone because objects are stored closer to users. For CloudFront to respect Amazon S3 cross-origin resource sharing settings, CloudFront must be configured to forward the Origin header to Amazon S3.

### Adding CloudFront to an existing S3 setup with your own domain name

If you distribute content from S3 using your own domain name, you can add CloudFront with no disruption by following the documented procedure. To keep using your own domain name to reference objects instead of the CloudFront domain name, you need to update your settings with your DNS service provider. For Amazon S3 CNAMEs to work, the DNS service provider must have a CNAME resource record set that currently routes queries for the domain to the S3 bucket. To route queries to CloudFront instead of S3, you must update the CNAME resource record set for your domain to point to the CloudFront domain name. If you use Route 53 as your DNS service, you can use either a CNAME resource record set or an alias resource record set.

After you update the CNAME resource record set, it can take up to 72 hours for the change to propagate throughout the DNS system, although it usually happens faster. During DNS propagation, some requests continue to be routed to the S3 bucket and others are routed to CloudFront.

### Moving a bucket to a different Region

CloudFront can take up to an hour to update its records for a moved bucket's new Region when both conditions hold: you use an origin access identity (OAI) to restrict bucket access, and you move the bucket to an S3 Region that requires Signature Version 4. When using OAIs, CloudFront uses the Region, among other values, to calculate the signature it uses to request objects from the bucket. Updating the CloudFront distribution, for example its Description field, forces a faster update because CloudFront immediately checks the Region of the bucket. Propagation of a distribution update to all edge locations should take only a few minutes.

## Application Load Balancers

CloudFront can route traffic to both internal and internet-facing Application Load Balancers. An internet-facing load balancer has a publicly resolvable DNS name and routes requests from clients to targets over the internet. VPC origins can deliver content from applications hosted with an internal Application Load Balancer in VPC private subnets and prevent the application from being accessible on the public internet.

## Network Load Balancers

You can use both internal and internet-facing Network Load Balancers with CloudFront. Internal Network Load Balancers inside private subnets can be used with CloudFront by using VPC origins.

## EC2 instances

You can use both internal and internet-facing EC2 instances with CloudFront, and internal instances in private subnets work via VPC origins. It is recommended to use an Elastic Load Balancing load balancer to handle traffic across multiple EC2 instances and isolate the application from EC2 instance changes. When using a load balancer in front of EC2 instances, you specify the load balancer URL as the domain name of the origin server.

## Lambda function URLs

A Lambda function URL is a dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a Lambda function. A Lambda web application can be invoked directly through the function URL with no need to integrate with API Gateway or an Application Load Balancer. To use a Lambda function URL as the origin, you specify the full domain name of the function URL as the origin domain. When using a Lambda function URL as an origin, the function URL must be publicly accessible.

If you use OAC with a Lambda function URL, the AuthType parameter must be AWS_IAM and a resource-based policy must allow lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions. If you don't use OAC, you can set the function URL AuthType to NONE and allow the lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl permission in a resource-based policy. Adding a custom origin header and writing function code to return an error if the header is absent helps ensure users can only access the web application through CloudFront and not directly via the Lambda function URL.

## Lambda Web Functions

A Lambda Web Function is a web application that runs on AWS Lambda and provides its own HTTPS endpoint, which can be regional or global. You can use a Lambda Web Function as the origin for a CloudFront distribution by specifying the hostname of its endpoint as the origin domain. A regional endpoint (HomeRegion and PerRegion types) has a hostname ending in .lambda-web.AWS-Region.on.aws, while a global endpoint (MultiRegion type) has a hostname ending in .lambda-web.global.on.aws.

To use OAC with a Lambda Web Function, the endpoint's auth type must be IamAuth, and the function's resource-based policy must allow the lambda:InvokeWebFunctionEndpoint permission. CloudFront signs requests to regional endpoints with SigV4 and to global endpoints with SigV4a.

## Custom origins

A custom origin is an HTTP(S) web server with a publicly resolvable DNS name that routes requests from clients to targets over the internet. Most CloudFront features are supported with a custom origin except private content. For CloudFront to access a custom origin, the origin must remain publicly accessible, even though signed URLs can be used to distribute content from it. CloudFront uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) for signed URLs, signed cookies, logs, and reports, and CloudWatch also uses UTC.

## Origin failover

Origin failover designates a primary origin plus a second origin that CloudFront automatically switches to when the primary origin returns specific HTTP status code failure responses. You can specify an origin group for your CloudFront origin to configure origin failover for high availability.

# Using origins with Amazon CloudFront

## Before you begin

Set up the following before the steps that need them.

- **S3 bucket with a DNS-compliant name** to hold the objects (the origin content bucket). Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/bucketnamingrules.html
- **S3 Object Lambda Access Point** (with its generated alias) to use as an origin. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/olap-create.html
- **S3 Access Point** (a supporting access point for Object Lambda, or an origin access point) to use as an origin. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/creating-access-points.html
- **AWS Lambda function** used by the Object Lambda Access Point.
- **CloudFront origin access control (OAC)**, required for Object Lambda and S3 Access Point origins. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html

## Origins overview

When you create a distribution, you specify the origin where CloudFront sends requests for the files. CloudFront can use an Amazon S3 bucket, a MediaStore container, a MediaPackage channel, an Application Load Balancer, or an AWS Lambda function URL as an origin. API Gateway can also be used as a custom origin. When you create a distribution, CloudFront automatically configures most distribution settings based on your content origin type.

You can use CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge to route requests to different origins based on factors such as the viewer's geographic location, request headers, or query string parameters.

For high availability, origin failover designates a primary origin plus a second origin that CloudFront automatically switches to when the primary origin returns specific HTTP status code failure responses. You configure it by specifying an origin group for your CloudFront origin; specifying an origin group is enough to set up origin failover.

## VPC origins

An Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer, or EC2 instance in a private subnet can be used as a VPC origin. With VPC origins, applications can be accessed only in a private subnet with a CloudFront distribution, which prevents the application from being accessible on the public internet. VPC origins can deliver content from applications hosted with an internal Application Load Balancer in VPC private subnets. Internal Network Load Balancers inside private subnets can be used with CloudFront by using VPC origins, and that is enough to keep the application off the public internet. Internal EC2 instances in private subnets likewise work via VPC origins.

## Amazon S3 buckets as origins

Using an existing Amazon S3 bucket as a CloudFront origin doesn't change the bucket in any way. You incur regular Amazon S3 charges for storing objects in the bucket. For the bucket to work with CloudFront, its name must conform to DNS naming requirements.

When specifying an S3 bucket as an origin, the recommended format is bucket-name.s3.region.amazonaws.com. With the bucket specified this way, you can:

- configure CloudFront to communicate with the bucket using SSL/TLS;
- use origin access control to require viewers to access content using CloudFront URLs rather than Amazon S3 URLs;
- update bucket content by submitting POST and PUT requests to CloudFront.

You should not specify the bucket using the path-style format s3.amazonaws.com/bucket-name or the Amazon S3 CNAME.

CloudFront supports S3 origins using any storage class, including S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Using CloudFront with S3 Intelligent-Tiering doesn't impact the performance or functionality of the distribution.

Using CloudFront can be more cost effective than serving directly from S3 if users access objects frequently, because at higher usage the CloudFront data transfer price is lower than the S3 data transfer price. Downloads are also faster with CloudFront than with Amazon S3 alone because objects are stored closer to users.

For CloudFront to respect Amazon S3 cross-origin resource sharing settings, CloudFront must be configured to forward the Origin header to Amazon S3.

## Object Lambda Access Points as origins

Amazon S3 automatically generates a unique alias for an Object Lambda Access Point when it is created, and you can use that alias instead of a bucket name as a CloudFront origin. When you use an Object Lambda Access Point as an origin, you must use origin access control; using OAC is enough for CloudFront to treat the origin the same as a standard Amazon S3 bucket origin. If you use Amazon S3 Object Lambda as an origin, you must configure four permissions: on the Object Lambda Access Point, the S3 Access Point, the S3 bucket, and the Lambda function.

## S3 Access Points as origins

Amazon S3 automatically generates a unique alias for an S3 Access Point, which can be used instead of a bucket name as a CloudFront origin. When you use an S3 Access Point as an origin, you must use origin access control, and that is enough for CloudFront to treat the origin the same as a standard Amazon S3 bucket origin.

## S3 website endpoints

An S3 bucket configured as a website endpoint can be used as a custom origin with CloudFront. An Amazon S3 origin configured as a website endpoint is considered a custom origin, which is enough for it to be used as one. When using the S3 website endpoint format as the origin, you can use Amazon S3 redirects and custom error documents. If you use the CloudFront API to create a distribution with an S3 bucket configured as a website endpoint, you must configure it by using CustomOriginConfig.

## S3 Multi-Region Access Points

An Amazon S3 Multi-Region Access Point can be used as a CloudFront origin. It provides a global endpoint that automatically routes requests to the closest S3 bucket based on network latency. You specify its hostname, multi-region-access-point-alias.accesspoint.s3-global.amazonaws.com, as the origin domain name.

## Moving from S3 to CloudFront with your own domain name

If you distribute content from S3 using your own domain name, you can add CloudFront with no disruption by following the documented procedure. To keep using your own domain name to reference objects instead of the CloudFront domain name, you need to update your settings with your DNS service provider.

For Amazon S3 CNAMEs to work, the DNS service provider must have a CNAME resource record set that currently routes queries for the domain to the S3 bucket. Only after that is in place do you update the CNAME resource record set for your domain to point to the CloudFront domain name, which routes queries to CloudFront instead of S3. If you use Route 53 as your DNS service, you can use either a CNAME resource record set or an alias resource record set.

After you update the record set, it can take up to 72 hours for the change to propagate throughout the DNS system, although it usually happens faster. During propagation, some requests continue to be routed to the S3 bucket and others are routed to CloudFront.

## Moving a bucket to another Region

CloudFront can take up to an hour to update its records for a moved bucket's new Region when both conditions hold: you use an origin access identity (OAI) to restrict bucket access and you move the bucket to an S3 Region that requires Signature Version 4. This applies only in that case, because when using OAIs CloudFront uses the Region, among other values, to calculate the signature it uses to request objects from the bucket. Updating the CloudFront distribution, for example its Description field, forces a faster update because CloudFront immediately checks the Region of the bucket. Propagation of a distribution update to all edge locations should take only a few minutes.

## Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers, and EC2

CloudFront can route traffic to both internal and internet-facing Application Load Balancers. An internet-facing load balancer has a publicly resolvable DNS name and routes requests from clients to targets over the internet. You can use both internal and internet-facing Network Load Balancers with CloudFront, and both internal and internet-facing EC2 instances.

It is recommended to use an Elastic Load Balancing load balancer to handle traffic across multiple EC2 instances and isolate the application from EC2 instance changes. When using a load balancer in front of EC2 instances, you specify the load balancer URL as the domain name of the origin server.

## Lambda function URLs

A Lambda function URL is a dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a Lambda function. A Lambda web application can be invoked directly through the function URL with no need to integrate with API Gateway or an Application Load Balancer. To use a function URL as the origin, you specify its full domain name as the origin domain. The function URL must be publicly accessible.

If you use OAC, the AuthType parameter must be AWS_IAM and a resource-based policy must allow lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions. If you don't use OAC, you can set the function URL AuthType to NONE and allow the lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl permission in a resource-based policy. Adding a custom origin header and writing function code to return an error if the header is absent helps ensure users can only access the web application through CloudFront and not directly via the function URL. This holds only when the function URL is publicly accessible and, with OAC, AuthType is AWS_IAM with the resource-based policy permissions in place.

## Lambda Web Functions

A Lambda Web Function is a web application that runs on AWS Lambda and provides its own HTTPS endpoint, which can be regional or global. You can use it as the origin for a CloudFront distribution by specifying the hostname of its endpoint as the origin domain. A regional endpoint (HomeRegion and PerRegion types) has a hostname ending in .lambda-web.AWS-Region.on.aws. A global endpoint (MultiRegion type) has a hostname ending in .lambda-web.global.on.aws.

To use OAC with a Lambda Web Function, the endpoint's auth type must be IamAuth, and the function's resource-based policy must allow the lambda:InvokeWebFunctionEndpoint permission. CloudFront signs requests to regional endpoints with SigV4 and to global endpoints with SigV4a.

## Custom origins

A custom origin is an HTTP(S) web server with a publicly resolvable DNS name that routes requests from clients to targets over the internet. Most CloudFront features are supported with a custom origin except private content. For CloudFront to access a custom origin, the origin must remain publicly accessible, even though signed URLs can be used to distribute content from it. That public accessibility is enough to explain the private content limitation. It also means a custom origin cannot be combined with the VPC origin guarantee of keeping an application off the public internet: the two cannot both hold.

CloudFront uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) for signed URLs, signed cookies, logs, and reports, and CloudWatch also uses UTC.
